description:
Team AstroNav

Solo entry developing a high reliability wearable health monitoring ecosystem for astronaut safety during long duration space missions.

Project Focus Building an integrated hardware and software solution that captures real time physiological data and delivers actionable health insights directly to astronauts.

Key Expertise Custom PCB fabrication, embedded systems, 3D structural design, and desktop telemetry software.
summary: AstroNav is health monitoring software that lets astronauts evaluate their own health and cabin air, and act on it immediately. Its core is a desktop console styled like the caution and warning panel on the ISS: it turns live health indicators into lamps, trends against a personal baseline and a body map linked to NASA’s hazards of human spaceflight, checks signal quality so bad readings are never shown as real, and gives one clear next step that it can send to the astronaut’s wrist. The data comes from AstroNav Wrist, a sensor watch I built on a custom PCB with an ESP32-S3: heart rate, SpO2, ECG with heart rate variability, skin conductance for stress, movement and tremor, plus cabin CO2, temperature and humidity. Following NASA-STD-3001, the crew is alerted both on the console and on the wrist. Movement is measured as motion rather than posture, because in microgravity there is no gravity reference. It matters because on long missions crews must spot stress, fatigue and air problems early, without waiting for ground control.
details:
What it does

AstroNav Wrist is a wrist station plus a desktop console that let a crew watch their own health and cabin air, and act on it without waiting for the ground.


The wrist station is a watch with a custom PCB, milled on a desktop CNC, in a 3D printed case. It measures:

  • Body: heart rate and SpO2 (MAX30102), ECG with RR intervals and heart rate variability (AD8232, chest electrodes), skin conductance for acute stress (GSR pads), and a skin temperature trend
  • Movement: activity, tremor, shock, and a double tap to acknowledge an alert (MPU-6050)
  • Cabin: real CO2, temperature and humidity (SCD41), and cabin pressure (BMP180)

The watch raises its own alarms, with a buzzer pattern per severity and the reason on the display, so the crew is warned even when the laptop is off. Seven days of minute summaries are stored on the watch.


The desktop console is built in the style of an ISS caution and warning panel:

  • one lamp per parameter, with the same classes as on the ISS, and the alarm sound can be muted per lamp
  • live ECG trace, vitals, and HRV against a personal baseline
  • cabin air with the NASA CO2 limit
  • a body map that links each body system to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight
  • a "What to do" panel that sends advice back to the wrist with one click
  • an event log, a seven day history pulled from the watch, and a crew selector

How it answers the challenge

The challenge asks for software that gathers health indicators and lets astronauts evaluate and act on them. AstroNav does that in three layers:

  • Gather: the firmware on AstroNav Wrist samples ECG, optical pulse, motion and skin conductance on one shared clock, measures the cabin air, and streams it all over my own Bluetooth protocol.
  • Evaluate: the console is where the astronaut sees their status: caution and warning lamps per parameter, heart rate variability against a personal baseline, cabin CO2 against the NASA limit, a seven day history, and a body map that links each body system to NASA’s hazards of human spaceflight.
  • Act: the “What to do” panel gives the most urgent next step in plain language and sends it to the wrist with one click; the astronaut confirms with a double tap.

It covers four of the five hazards: isolation and confinement (stress from HRV and skin conductance), altered gravity (heart, activity, tremor), the hostile closed environment (cabin CO2 against NASA-STD-3001, oxygen saturation) and distance from Earth (the crew does not depend on the ground). Cardiovascular events and behavioral health are watched directly; bone loss and immune changes only indirectly, through activity and skin temperature trends. Space radiation is not covered yet; a dosimeter is the next step.

How it works

The watch speaks its own compact Bluetooth Low Energy protocol: raw streams, vitals, air, cabin, status and alert events. ECG, optical pulse, motion and skin conductance share one 4 ms clock, so heart rate variability and a future blood pressure trend line up. There is no OS pairing: the console unlocks the watch with the six digit code shown on its screen. A Rust backend parses the packets and a React interface shows them.

Benefits and intended impact

On long missions, help from Earth is slow or out of reach. Crews need to notice stress, poor sleep, heart changes and bad air themselves, early, and know what to do next. AstroNav Wrist puts that on the wrist and on one console screen.

Impact on Earth

The same problem exists wherever people work isolated, in a closed space, far from a doctor: polar stations, submarines, offshore platforms, mines, and also patients at home or in places with few clinics. Badly ventilated rooms with high CO2 are common in classrooms and offices too. Because AstroNav is built from low cost parts that anyone can buy, with open source firmware, software and hardware, it can be copied and adapted for these places. Anyone can build their own watch. The schematic and PCB design are open on OSHWLab: https://oshwlab.com/youphoutkamp/project_ougymktu. The PCB Gerbers and the STL files of the 3D printed case are in the main repo, together with a list of the known issues of this PCB revision. Software is licensed under GPL-3.0, hardware under CERN-OHL-S v2.

Science and validation

I tested every claim on real hardware and changed the design when the data said so. The optical SpO2 was compared against a real pulse oximeter. When the wrist showed falsely low values during movement, I traced it to motion and weak perfusion, and the watch now drops those readings instead of raising a false alarm. ECG noise was studied with raw sample dumps, and RR intervals from a clipped or noisy signal are excluded from heart rate variability. Every alarm limit has a stated source: NASA-STD-3001 for the cabin, the WHO Pulse Oximetry Training Manual for SpO2, and where no standard exists, it is labelled as my own choice.

From prototype to mission

The design is plausible for a real mission: it follows the crew alerting architecture that NASA-STD-3001 asks for, it keeps working without the laptop or the ground, and it stores seven days of data on the watch for trend analysis. The next steps are clear: a battery, a radiation dosimeter for the one hazard I do not cover yet, and a console that shows the whole crew side by side.


What makes it creative

  • Designed for microgravity. On Earth a wearable uses gravity as a reference to tell posture and count steps. In space that reference is gone, so AstroNav Wrist measures motion (activity, tremor, shock) instead of posture.
  • NASA's own rules. The architecture follows NASA-STD-3001: the CO2 limit, and alerting the crew locally on the wrist as well as remotely on the console.
  • Honest data. Optical readings during movement or weak perfusion are dropped, and RR intervals from a noisy ECG are ignored. Every simulated value in demo mode is flagged on the watch (*) and in the console ("Sim").


Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Hardware: Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3, MAX30102, AD8232, MPU-6050, SCD41, BMP180, 0.96" OLED, piezo buzzer, custom PCB (desktop CNC), 3D printed case
  • Firmware: C++ with PlatformIO (Arduino core)
  • Console: Tauri 2, Rust (btleplug), React, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest

Why I built this

Being part of space has been my dream since I was young. At home, space is what keeps me busy, for example building my own flight controllers for model rockets. When I saw this challenge, I knew I could make it something special by building a real wearable next to the software. I designed the PCB, milled it, soldered it and printed the case myself, all in one weekend. Not everything went to plan, and every setback is listed honestly below. I hope my work inspires others, so I am sharing everything openly: the firmware, the console and the hardware.

Factors I considered

  • Sensor choice by NASA limits: the SCD41 instead of the SCD40, because the SCD40's range does not reach NASA's CO2 limit.
  • Alerts on both the console and the wrist, as NASA-STD-3001 asks, so the crew is warned even if one of them is not in view.
  • Physiological limits are marked as advice, not a diagnosis.

Honest limitations of the prototype:

  • It runs on USB, because the battery connector broke during the build.
  • There is no light sensor.
  • Skin temperature is a trend, not a fever reading.
  • Wrist SpO2 is less accurate than a fingertip.
  • The ECG heart rate is not yet reliable.
  • There is no ppO2 or radiation sensor.
  • Only one real watch can connect at a time; the other crew members are demo watches.
  • The cabin pressure sensor on my unit gives impossible readings, so there is no pressure or leak alarm yet.

Try it yourself

A Windows installer of the console is on the releases page of the main repo: https://github.com/youptheking/SpaceApps2026-AstroNav-Dashboard/releases/latest. Without a watch, turn on Demo in the top bar to see a five minute scenario on simulated data.

Use of AI

The idea and concept are my own. Claude (Anthropic) was used to research parts, look up limits in NASA-STD-3001, draft documentation, and write a significant portion of the code from my own design. PCB design, milling, soldering, the case and all testing on the real watch were done by hand. This is also stated in the “Use of AI” section of both READMEs.
